speaker: Doctor
text: Good morning, I see you are experiencing double vision, difficulty climbing stairs, and weakness in your upper limbs. To understand the severity and location of your neurological deficit, have you noticed any muscle weakness in your legs or hands, or any numbness in your fingers or toes?

speaker: Patient
text: The double vision usually happens when I look up or down, and the weakness in my arms and legs gets worse after activity but improves if I rest. I have not noticed balance problems or numbness.

speaker: Doctor
text: The pattern of double vision worsening with up/down gaze and weakness improving with rest is very specific. To confirm if this is a neuromuscular junction disorder, do you experience drooping eyelids or a slurred speech that fluctuates throughout the day?

speaker: Patient
text: I have not had recent infections or fevers, and there is no family history of neurological disease. The weakness feels symmetrical in both arms and legs.

speaker: Doctor
text: DIAGNOSIS READY: Myasthenia Gravis. The combination of fatigable diplopia (worse looking up/down), proximal limb weakness that improves with rest, and the absence of sensory deficits or fever is classic for this neuromuscular junction disorder. I am confident this is the diagnosis without needing further testing.
